entities.label: Text
entities.summary: Section 11 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1885, commonly known as the Labouchère Amendment, made "gross indecency" a crime in the United Kingdom. In practice, the law was used broadly to prosecute male homosexuals where actual sodomy could not be proven. The penalty of life imprisonment for sodomy was also so harsh that successful prosecutions were rare. The new law was much more enforceable. In England and Wales, section 11 was repealed and re-enacted by section 13 of the Sexual Offences Act 1956; this in turn was repealed by the Sexual Offences Act 1967, which partially decriminalised male homosexual behaviour.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Labouchère Amendment significantly impacted LGBTQ+ rights in the UK, contributing to a culture of fear and persecution that lasted for decades. It was not until the Sexual Offences Act 1967 that male homosexual behavior was partially decriminalized.
